I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut of  by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth.’ And God said, ‘This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.’

God said to Noah, ‘This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.’

The sons of Noah who went forth from the Ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan. These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father’s nakedness. When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, he said, ‘Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.’ He also said, ‘Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.’ After the flood Noah lived 350 years. All the days of Noah were 950 years, and then he died. A Discussion of the Biblical Account:

As you can observe, this narrative contradicts the Qurʾan from a number of aspects:

Firstly, it does not mention the exception of Noah’s wife; instead, it explicitly states that she boarded the ark and was saved with her husband. Some have sought to rationalise this apparent incongruity by suggesting that Noah may have had two wives—one who drowned, and one who survived.

Secondly, it omits the account of Noah’s son who drowned, which is narrated in the Qurʾan.

Thirdly, it does not mention any believers other than Noah and his family, restricting the account to him, his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons.

Fourthly, it cites Noah’s total lifespan as nine hundred and fifty years, while the Qurʾan indicates that this was merely the period he spent preaching among his people, inviting them to God before the flood. As God

says, “ Certainly We sent Noah to his people, and he remained with them for a thousand-less-fifty years. Then the flood overtook them while they were wrongdoers. (29:14)

Fifthly, it mentions the appearance of a rainbow, describes Noah sending out a raven and a dove to investigate, and includes details such as the

ark’s dimensions—its length, width, height, its three levels—the flood’s duration, the water’s elevation, and other specifics which are not mentioned in the Qurʾan. Some of these details seem far-fetched and unlikely,

such as the divine covenant symbolized by the rainbow. Many of these elements have found their way into Islamic accounts of Noah’s story through narrations transmitted by the Companions and Successors, and the majority of these appear to borrowings from Jewish and Christian sources (Isrāʾīliyyāt).

Accounts of the Flood in Different World Cultures:

The author of Tafsīr al-Manār highlights that accounts of the Flood have appeared in the annals of various ancient civilizations and nations. Some of these accounts broadly align in their details with the narrative found in Genesis, while others differ from it significantly The narrative closest to this is that of the Chaldeans, who experienced the flood in their own land. It is narrated by the Babylonian chronicler Berossus and the Roman-Jewish historian Josephus that the Sumerian king Xisuthrus dreamt, following his father Otiartes’ death, that water would overwhelm and drown all of humanity. He was instructed to build an ark in which he, his family, and especially his friends could seek refuge, which he did. This aligns with the Genesis narrative, wherein there was a generation of giants on earth, who were corrupt and filled the world with wickedness, for which God punished them with a flood.

An English Assyriologist, George Smith (d. 1876) discovered clay tablets inscribed with this narrative in cuneiform from the reign of the Neo-

Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, around six hundred and sixty years before the birth of Christ. These were transcriptions from an older script dating back to the seventeenth century B.C. or earlier, which would make them older than the Book of Genesis.

The Greeks have a flood narrative that Plato recounts in Timaeus: the Egyptian priests told Solon, the Greek philosopher, that the heavens had sent a flood that altered the earth’s surface, destroying humanity multiple times through various means. Nothing remained of the previous generation’s landmarks or knowledge for subsequent generations.

The Egyptian priest Manetho narrates a flood account that occurred after the first Hermes, who came after M enes I. This account predates the Torah. Ancient Greeks also told the story of a global flood, from which only Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived.

Ancient Persians narrated a flood narrative, in which God drowned the earth due to the rampant corruption and evils spread by Ahriman, the god of darkness and evil. They claim the flood began as waters surged from the oven of an old woman while she was baking her bread. However, the Zoroastrians did not believe that this flood covered the entirety of the earth, asserting it was confined to the region of Iraq and ended at the borders of Kurdistan.

Similarly, ancient Indian legends affirm the occurrence of the flood seven times, in a mythic form. The last of these accounts tells of their king and his wife surviving in a great ship, which their god had commanded them to build. The ship was launched and filled with pitch until it came to rest on the Himalayas. But, like the Zoroastrians, the Brahmans deny a global flood, instead saying that it merely drowned all of India. Flood accounts have can also be found from Japan, China, Brazil, Mexico, and other places. All these narratives concur that the cause of such a cataclysm was God’s punishment for human oppression and wickedness.

In the Zoroastrian holy book, the Avesta, it is recorded that Ahura Mazda revealed to Yima (whom the Zoroastrians believe to be the ancient Persian king Jamshid) that a flood would engulfithe earth. He was commanded to construct a high wall to protect those inside from drowning.

He was to gather within it a group of men and women suitable for procreation, introduce two of every kind of animal species, and build houses

and domes in various layers for the assembled people to live in and provide refuge for the animals and birds. He was also instructed to plant fruit trees and cultivate crops to sustain human life and allow them to repopulate the world after the waters had subsided.

In ancient Indian legends1 there is a flood story in which Manu (whom they believed to be the son of God) was washing his hands when a fish appeared. Manu was amazed when the fish spoke, asking to be saved from destruction, and promising in return to save Manu from a great danger in the future. The fish foretold that a great flood would come and sweep away all creatures. Consequently, M anu kept the fish safe in a jar. When the fish grew, it informed Manu about the year the flood would occur and instructed him to build a large ship, which he should board to remain safe during the deluge. The fish promised to save him from the flood. Manu constructed the ship, and as the fish grew larger than the jar could accommodate, he released it into the sea.

The flood occurred as the fish had predicted. When Manu entered the ship, the fish swam towards him, and he fastened the ship to a horn on its head. It pulled him towards the northern mountains, where Manu tied the ship to a tree. As the water receded and dried up, M anu remained alone. Was Noah’s prophethood universal for all humankind?

The question of whether Noah was a prophet for all humankind is a matter on which scholars have differing views. Among the Shīʿa, it is commonly believed that his message was universal and intended for all humankind. This view is supported by traditions narrated from the Household of

1 According to the Qiṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ of ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Najjār. (Auth.) the Prophet that suggest that Those Endowed with Resolve (ūlū al-ʿazm)— including Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad—were sent to all humanity.

As for the Sunnī school of thought, some scholars assert that Noah’s message was universal, relying on the apparent meaning of verses that speak of the flood afiecting all the inhabitants of the earth. Such verses include God’s statement: ‘Do not leave on the earth any inhabitant from among the faithless’ (71:26), His saying, ‘There is none today who can protect from Allah’s edict, except someone upon whom He has mercy.’ (11:43), and His statement: and made his descendants the survivors (37: 77). This view also draws on a tradition from sources they deem authentic that Noah was the first Messenger sent by God to the people of the earth, suggesting his mission was to all of them.

However, other Sunnī scholars reject this based on a tradition in the Saḥīḥ from the Prophet: ‘Each Prophet was sent specifically to his people - and I was sent to all of mankind.’ These scholars say that the aforementioned verses should be interpreted with this in mind. It is plausible, they

argue, that ‘the earth’ mentioned in the verses refers only to the land inhabited by Noah’s people, their homeland, as when Pharaoh said to Moses

and Aaron, ‘…so that supremacy may be yours in the land (al-ard)?’ (10:78). This could render the meaning of the first verse: ‘Leave not one disbeliever of my people on this earth.’ The second could mean: ‘None can

protect my people from God’s edict today,’ and the third could mean: ‘And We made his descendants the survivors of his people.’

However, the reality is that this topic has not been fully explored in their discussions. W hat must, at the very least, be stated is that prophethood emerged in human society in response to a genuine need for it and

a real bond between people and their Lord. It is based on a cosmic reality rather than being an arbitrary matter of convention. One of the real

principle operating within the cosmic order is that all species must move towards perfection and be guided towards their existential goals. God says, …who created and proportioned, who determined and guided (87:3-4), and also, … who gave everything its creation and then guided it (20:50). In other words, every kind of being, from the moment of its inception, is directed towards the perfection of its existence and the goal of its creation, wherein lies its ultimate good and happiness. The human species is

no exception to this principle; its individuals and communities are directed towards their perfection and happiness. Moreover, it is crucial to note that such perfection cannot be achieved by the human being alone, given his numerous vital needs and the myriad tasks that must be performed to meet them. The practical intellect, which drives him to benefit from everything possible and utilise inanimate objects, plants, and animals for his own benefit, also encourages him to benefit from the works of other members of his own species by cooperating with them.

And yet, individuals are all alike, each possessing the same practical intellect and unique human sensibilities as the other. These spur them to cooperate with one another: Everyone works for the collective good and profits from the works of others to the extent that they contribute their own efforts. God says, It is We who have dispensed among them their livelihood in the present life, and raised some of them above others in rank, so that

some may take others into service (43:32).

This is what we mean when we say that human beings are fundamentally built for collaborative association. The necessities of life and our social

dynamics compel us to function as cooperative beings. Despite this, human nature’s primary instinct is to maximise the benefit they derive from anything that presents them with an opportunity to do so, even if this the

efforts of other people. Thus, regardless of how strong or self-sufficient a person may become, if they start to exploit others without compensation, this only confirms God’s words: Indeed man is most unfair and ungrateful! (14:34) and Indeed man becomes rebellious when he considers himself

without need. Indeed to your Lord is the return (96: 8).

M oreover, it is essential to realize that collaborative associations among individual human beings can only arise through the establishment of laws to govern these associations and guardians to enforce them. This is demonstrated by the continuous historical trajectory of human societies. Regardless of how complete or deficient, sophisticated or primitive a

society may be, there exist customs and norms wholly or mostly observed. History, experience, and observation all attest to this simple fact. These customs, norms, or, if you prefer, laws, are mental concepts that are applied either entirely or mostly in society, resulting in happiness either in reality or at least in perception. These laws are elements that are integral to

the human pursuit of perfection, and they provide a course for humans to follow in their transition from a primal state to a complete form living in society. They guide humans towards the ultimate purpose of their

existence.

We understand it to be a matter of divine necessity for God to guide humans towards the fulfilment of their life’s purpose and the perfection of their existence, just as He guides all other species towards these goals. As such, He has guided them through their own nature and instinct to seek their wellbeing and happiness; through the order of the universe and the faculties with which He has furnished them and which allow them to distinguish benefit from harm, good from evil, and happiness from misery. As God says, by the soul and Him who fashioned it,and inspired it with its virtues and vices: one who purifies it is felicitous, and one who betrays

it fails (91:7–10).

God guides humanity, through His necessary care (ʿināya), towards the foundational and practical principles of belief and action. The application of these principles completes and fulfils the human’s life purpose.

God’s divine care for the perfection of all species, in accordance with their unique nature, necessitates this kind of guidance, as does it the guidance towards purely physical fiourishing also.

However, the intellect with which the human being has been equipped, as useful as it may be, is not by itself sufficient in this respect. As we have already discussed, the intellect incites us to make use of things for our benefit and to discern one thing from another. Now, it is impossible for one faculty to perform two opposing actions or to yield two contradictory results. Nevertheless, those individuals who disregard society’s laws and commit crimes against others are still rational beings, who benefit from the faculties of reason.

Thus, it becomes clear that there must be another path for teaching humanity the truth of the divine law and showing them the path of perfection and happiness in addition to that of thinking and intellect: This

is the path of revelation. This divine form of communication conveys to humans what will lead them to success by acting on it and believing in it, both in this worldly life and in the Hereafter.

Now, one might argue that revelation makes no difference, for the law of the prophets does not provide anything more than what reason can: humanity will refuse to submit to the laws of the prophets as surely as it has refused to submit to the laws of the intellect. Therefore, if revelation cannot direct human society or guide it to the path of truth, what use is it? To this, I would respond by saying that this discussion has two dimensions. The first is that it is a divine necessity to guide human society through

teachings that would cause people to flourish and be fulfilled if they are followed—this is the guidance of revelation, and reason by itself is not enough here. The second dimension is the question of what the external reality and actual situation is. Our focus in this discussion is on the first dimension, and the fact that this prophethood has scarcely led people towards its intended purpose does not in any way diminish our argument. This is akin to how God’s care guides plant and animal species towards the perfection of their creation and the purpose of their existence. Yet, most individuals of each species fall short of reaching their species-specific purpose and perish before attaining their natural lifespan.

In summary, the path of prophethood and revelation is indispensable for the cultivation and nurturing of mankind when considering God’s care for His creatures. W ithout revelation, God’s argument over mankind would not be complete based solely on reason, for it has a role beyond this scope, namely calling humans towards what is in their own best interest. Even if it calls them towards something beneficial for the species, it does so because of its relevance to their individual wellbeing. Understand this, and consider carefully God’s words: We have indeed revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and (as) We revealed to Abraham and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, Jesus and Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon,—and We gave David the Psalms—and messengers W e have recounted to you earlier and messengers W e have not recounted to you,— and to M oses Allah spoke directly— messengers, as bearers of good news and warners, so that mankind may not have any argument against Allah, after the (sending of the) messengers; and Allah is all-mighty, allwise (4:163–165).

Therefore, it is a necessary and logical corollary of God’s care and concern for His creatures that He reveals a religion for human society to follow

and a code of laws for them to observe in their social lives, without focusing only some groups and leaving others aside without care. The necessary

implication of this is that the first code of law revealed to humankind— meaning the laws brought by Noah—must be a universal law.

God has informed us of this universal principle in His saying, ‘Mankind were a single community; then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good news and as warners, and He sent down with them the Book with the truth, that it may judge between the people concerning that about which they differed

(2:213). This indicates that people were initially and naturally a single body, showing no signs of conflicts or disputes. Then, when differences emerged among them, God sent prophets with a code of laws and a scripture with which to judge truthfully in those matters they differed in, and to settle the subjects of contention and dispute that existed between them.

As for the special favor that God showed to the Prophet Muḥammad, He says in the Qurʾan, He has prescribed for you the religion which He had enjoined upon Noah and which We have revealed to you, and which We had enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus (42:13). The context of this verse suggests that the divine laws revealed to all of humanity are those mentioned and no others. The first law mentioned is that of Noah. Had it not been universal for all humans, especially in his time, there would have been another prophet with another law for those other than Noah’s people, and such a prophet has not been mentioned in this verse or in any other place in the Qurʾan. And if Noah’s law was not universal and no such prophet was sent, then this would have meant that God had neglected the rest of humankind who were not part of Noah’s people, both at his time and thereafter.

Therefore, it is clear that Noah’s mission as a prophet was universal, and he was given a book that contained a code of laws that was intended to eliminate disagreements. His book was the first of the heavenly scriptures containing the divine law. The part of the aforementioned verse which says, and He sent down with them the Book with the truth, that it may judge between the people concerning that about which they differed, refers to his book, or to his book alongside the books of other Resolute Prophets: Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad.

It also appears that any indication found in the traditions that his call was not universal contradicts the explicit meaning of the Qurʾan. For example, in a tradition from Imām al-Riḍā, we read: ‘Those Endowed with Resolve are five in number. Each of them had a code of laws and a book, and their prophetic mission was universal for everyone besides them, whether these were prophets or not.’ We have already discussed this tradition in our commentary on the verse, Mankind were a single community (2:213).

Did the flood cover the entirety of the earth?

The answer to this question was clarified in the previous chapter. The universality of Noah’s prophetic mission necessitates the universality of the divine punishment. This is indeed an excellent indication that all the verses that appear to indicate the global nature of the Flood do in fact point to this. For example, when God recounts statements from Noah such as, ‘Do not leave on the earth any inhabitant from among the faithless’ (71:26), His saying, ‘There is none today who can protect from Allah’s edict, except someone upon whom He has mercy.’ (11:43), and God’s own statement: and made his descendants the survivors (37: 77).

Further evidence for the Flood being worldwide can be found in two places in the Qurʾan. First, when God commanded Noah to load two of every species of animal into the Ark, when it is clear that if the Flood was a localized event— for example, to Iraq, as has been suggested— there would have been no need to carry two of every single species in the Ark—as should be obvious.

In spite of this, some scholars have argued that the flood was localized to the land of Noah’s people. For example, Rāshid Riḍā, the author of the commentary al-M anār, argues exactly this. For instance, after discussing the salvation of Noah and his family, speaks about the verse, and made his descendants the survivors (37: 77). He says that while the phrase ‘the survivors’ (al-bāqīn) might imply the meaning of ‘the onlysurvivors’, this could mean ‘the onlysurvivorsofihis people.’ As for when Noah said, ‘Do not leave on the earth any inhabitant from among the faithless’, Rāshid Riḍā says that ‘the earth’ (al-arḍ) here need not refer to the entirety of the globe, as it is often the case in the stories of various prophets and nations that the term al-arḍ is used to denote their land or homeland. For example, God recounts Pharaoh telling Moses and Aaron: ‘… so that supremacy may be yours in the land (al-arḍ)?’ (10:78) Here, Pharaoh uses al-arḍ to refer to the land of Egypt. Equally, consider the verse addressed to the Prophet, They were about to hound you out of the land (al-arḍ), to expel you from it (17:76), where al-arḍ refers to the land of M ecca. Then there is the verse, W e decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book: ‘Twice you will cause corruption in the land (al-arḍ), and you will perpetrate great tyranny’ (17:4), where the meaning of al-arḍ is their homeland. According to him, there are many examples of this.

Moreover, he argues that the apparent meaning of the verses, combined with contextual evidence and the accounts received from the People

of the Book, indicate that during Noah’s time, his people were the only ones alive on Earth. All of them were wiped out by the Flood, and only his descendants remained afterwards. This suggests that the Flood must have occurred in the area of the earth in which they lived, covering its plains and mountains, but not the entire planet. Unless of course the dry land at that time was minimal due to its relatively recent formation and the even more recent emergence of humans on it. Indeed, scholars of formation and geological strata suggest that when Earth separated from the Sun, it was a fiery, infiamed sphere. It then became a watery sphere, and dry land gradually emerged on it over millions of years.

Next, he highlights the evidence presented by some thinkers that the Flood covered the entire Earth. They claimed that the presence of certain seashells and fossilized fish at the tops of mountains, which can only form in the sea, indicates that water once reached these heights. This could only have occurred if the water had indeed covered the Earth.

However, he rejects this argument because the presence of seashells and marine animals at the tops of mountains does not necessarily indicate that this was due to that Flood. Instead, it is more likely that this was a result of the formation of mountains and other dry land in water, as previously mentioned. After all, a few days would not provide sufficient time for the waters to reach such heights.

Finally, Rashīd Riḍā argues to the effect that these historical issues are not the primary objectives of the Qurʾan. Therefore, they were not clarified with any definitive verses. As a result, he maintains what he has previously stated as an apparent explanation of the texts, but he does not adopt it as a definitive religious belief. He goes on to say that if geological science proves otherwise, it would not afiect his religious beliefs, because such scientific findings do not contradict any explicit text in his belief system. Author’s comment: In response to the views of Rashīd Riḍā: His interpretation of these verses is an arbitrary restriction of the meaning of the text, without any evidence to support it. Likewise, his rejection of seashells and fish being found on mountain tops as evidence for a global flood—because a few days would not have given sufficient time for the waters to rise so high— is vulnerable to counter-arguments, because it is entirely possible that these remains were carried to such heights by the waves of the Flood and remained there after the water receded. It is also not necessarily impossible for a Flood to submerge towering mountains within a few days.

In addition to this, Rashīd Riḍā has ignored what the verses do make explicit, namely that Noah was ordered to take two of each kind of animal species. This is virtually a clear declaration that the Flood would cover all, or most, of the Earth’s dry lands, the majority being tantamount to all. The truth is that the apparent meaning of the Qurʾan—a meaning that is, in fact, undeniable—is that the Flood was global and that all human beings on Earth were drowned save for those aboard the Ark with Noah. No definitive argument has yet arisen that could divert the text from this apparent meaning.

These were originally sharp-edged, angular pieces of stone that were gradually smoothed by the friction caused by them colliding together in running water and great floods. The water then carried them and spread them on the Earth, depositing them in both nearby or distant locations.

Sedimentary lands are not limited to plains. M ost terrains of this type are mixed with or formed of extremely fine sand. Because of its fineness and lightness, this sand was transported to far of  locations by the flow of

This suggests that the sedimentary lands were once channels and pathways for significant amounts of water and large floods, even though they

From what has been mentioned, it can be deduced firstly, that the earth’s surface was not too long ago (as will be discussed further) regularly experienced enormous floods that may have covered most or all of its plains. Secondly, considering the thickness of the sedimentary crust in some places, the flood did not occur once or within a single year or a few years. Instead, it lasted or repeated over hundreds of years. Each time it occurred, it formed a sedimentary layer, then, if it stopped, a layer of soil covered it. If it recurred, it formed another layer, and so forth. Sedimentary layers are the youngest geological crusts and strata: Sedimentary layers usually settle horizontally. However, their accumulated parts might have been subject to intense pressures from above and below. As a result, they gradually shift from a straight horizontal orientation and become curved or twisting. This effect is not apparent over short periods but becomes more noticeable over the course of millions of years. As a result, mountains and their twisting ranges are formed, with some of their hills overlapping each other and their peaks rising above sea levels. From this, we can infer that the surviving horizontal sedimentary layers and crusts are among the most recent strata to be formed on the earth’s surface. The available technical evidence suggests that they were not formed more than ten to fifteen thousand years before our present time.1 3. The expansion of the seas: It appears that the new sedimentary crusts have played a role in the expansion of most of the world’s seas. Their waters rose and covered most of their coasts, forming islands surrounded by the sea on most sides.

For example, it was during this time that the British Isles became entirely separated from France and the rest of Europe. Europe became separated from Africa on its southern side and Africa from Europe on its northern side, where the two had previously been connected by land, due to the expansion of the M editerranean Sea. The Indonesian islands from Java and Sumatra side to southern Japan, which had been connected to Asia from the south-east until now, became separated and assumed their current form. Similarly, the separation of North America from Northern Europe is one of the remaining effects of this period – the era of the Flood.

The internal movements and transformations of the earth have had effects on the flow of these waters and how they have settled in the depressions on the earth’s surface. This is why the water receded from some

submerged coastal areas when the Flood dominated most of the surface, forming lakes and expanding seas. An example of this is the southern coast of Khuzestan, from which the waters of the Persian Gulf receded.2 4. These incessant and heavy rains, which fell on elevations and in valleys, especially on the newly-formed mountain ranges in southern and

What contributed to the intensity of the Flood and added to the intensity of its waters was that the excavation of new valleys revealed additional

The Qurʾan indicates that Noah lived a long life and that he invited his people to worship God for a thousand years minus fifty. Some researchers have dismissed this due to human lifespan generally not exceeding one

The reason for the Flood

still wisdom in God’s decree.

On Idol Worship

Human beings and their reliance on sense perception A human being, in their social life, acts on the basis of the law of cause and effect and other universal laws that they have derived from observing the cosmic order. In this, they differ from the behavior of other animals, because they engage in reflection and deduction—by which I mean logical reasoning— in order to achieve long-term goals.

And yet, human beings cannot feel confidence in their examination and inquiry without forming a verdict regarding the cause of this observable world, of which they are a part, whether afiirmatively or negatively. This is because they realize that their life’s happiness, which they desire above anything else, fundamentally differs based on whether they affirm or deny the existence of this agent known as God. It is obvious that there can be no comparison between the life of a human being who affirms the existence of a living, knowledgeable, and capable Creator for the world, who inevitably submits to His greatness and majesty and lives his life according to what He loves and approves of, and the life of a human being who views the world as aimless, without a beginning or an end, and where human life is but a limited existence that perishes with death and is nullified by passing, and humanity has no higher purpose in it except what animals have in terms of lust, anger, and the desire for food and sex.

Therefore, there is an innate intellectual tendency in humans to ask the question: Is there a God? This is followed by a second tendency, which is the innate tendency to affirm and decide that there is a God who created everything in existence with His power and set the cosmic order in motion with His Lordship, guiding everything towards its goal and perfecting its existence in accordance with His will, and that everything that exists will ultimately return to its Lord just as it originated from Him.

Moreover, a human’s constant engagement with perception and what is perceptible throughout their life, their immersion in materiality, and their attachment to the earth all lead them to represent everything they understand and imagine in a tangible perceptible form, even if it something completely inaccessible to perception and imagination, such as universal principles and abstract truths that are detached from matter. However, humans gain an understanding of objects of intellect through their faculties of sense and imagination— two faculties on which they rely extensively

in their thought.

This inherent human tendency means that one often imagines gives their God an imaginary form based on what they are familiar with from tangible, physical matters. Even most monotheists, who believe in the utter transcendence and sanctity of the Lord of the Worlds above the limits of physicality and its conditions, establish in their minds a vague, imaginary image of Him that is separate from the world. This image comes to mind when they turn to Him regarding a matter or speak about Him. However, religious education rectifies this by establishing a balance between negation and affirmation and by drawing a distinction between anthropomorphism and transcendence. The monotheistic Muslim says: ‘He is something unlike anything else, He has power unlike the power of His creation, and knowledge unlike any other knowledge’—and so on, in this fashion.

Rarely does it happen that a human turns towards the realm of divinity and majesty, with their self being free from this anthropomorphic tendency. It is even more unusual for there to be a person who has devoted

himself utterly to God, with his heart unattached to anything other than Him, and who is untouched by satanic anthropomorphisms. God has said: Clear is Allah of whatever they allege, except Allah’s exclusive servants

(37:160). He has also related that Iblis said: ‘By Your might, I will surely pervert them, except Your exclusive servants among them’ (38:83).

In summary, humans are strongly inclined to imagine non-perceptible matters in the form of perceptible things. So, when they hear that there is something beyond physical nature that is stronger, more capable, greater, and higher than nature, and that it is active in it, which encompasses it, predates it, manages it, and rules it, such that nothing comes into being but by its command, and nothing changes from one state to another except by its will and decision, they can only initially comprehend this by analogy to their understanding of physical attributes.

Often, they imagine it in their minds as a human figure above the heavens, seated on a majestic throne, governing the affairs of the world through his contemplation, directing them by his will and issuing commands and prohibitions. The existing Torah explicitly states that God is

so, and that He created humans in His image, and the Gospels also appear to indicate this as well.

It so happens that it is a feature of human nature, especially in primitive early humans, is to create an image for their God, who is free from

similarity and comparison, that resembles physical beings and matches the descriptions and attributes they ascribe to Him, just as they represent the Trinity as a human with three faces, as if each of the general attributes is a face of the Lord turning towards His creation with it.

Turning towards the worship of God:

When a person determines that the cosmos has a deity who created it through His knowledge and power, it is inevitable that he will submit to Him through the humility of worship, in accordance with the universal law of the cosmos. This law is the submission of the weak to the strong, the obedience of the powerless to the powerful, and the surrender of the lesser to the greater. This is a general law that governs all aspects of existence

and afiects causes and their effects.

When this law becomes evident to beings endowed with senses and will, such as animals, it sets a precedent for submission and obedience of the weak to the strong. This can be observed in the behavior of animals when the weaker ones recognise the superiority of the stronger ones and give up any resistance or opposition to them.

This law becomes manifest in the human world in a way that is broader and more apparent than in any other creature due to the depth of the human being’s cognition and his capacity for rational thought. In fact, it can be observed in most of our goals and actions, where we rely on it to seek benefit or avoid harm. Examples of this include subjects submitting to their ruler, the poor to the rich, the subordinate to the leader, the commanded to the commander, the servant to the served, the student to the

teacher, the lover to the beloved, the needy to the afiiuent, the slave to the master, and the creature to the Creator.

All of these relationships of submission are, in fact, one and the same. They represent psychological humility and abasement before something that is perceived to be greater and more dominant. The physical act that embodies and exemplifies this humility is worship, no matter to whom or by whom it is performed. There is no distinction in this regard between submission to the Almighty God, to a master by a slave, to a ruler by the subjects, or to the afiiuent by the needy: In reality, all of these acts of submission are forms of worship.

In any case, there is no way to deter a person from submitting themselves in this way, because it is based on an innate judgement from which

humans cannot deviate unless they realize that which they believed was powerful and before which they abased themselves was not greater than them as they assumed, but merely their own equal, for instance.

Hence, we observe that Islam did not prohibit the worship of deities other than God until it demonstrated to people that these deities were created beings like them, and that all power and glory belonged to God alone. As said in the Qurʾan, in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, Indeed those whom you invoke besides Allah are creatures like you (7:194); Those whom you invoke besides Him can neither help you, nor help themselves. If you call them to guidance, they will not hear. You see them observing you, but they do not perceive (7:198).

Meanwhile, in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān, God says, Say, ‘O People of the Book! Come to a word common between us and you: that we will worship no one but Allah, and that we will not ascribe any partner to Him, and that we will not take each other as lords besides Allah.’ But if they turn away, say, “Be witnesses that we are muslims.’ (3:64) This verse concludes by telling the faithful to affirm their submission to God after instructing them to refrain from worshipping other deities and rejecting submission to all beings who are created like themselves. In Sūrah al-Baqarah, we read: power, altogether, belongs to Allah (2:165); while Sūrah al-Nisāʾ says, indeed all honor belongs to Allah (4:139); and Sūrah al-Sajda reads, You do not have besides Him any guardian or intercessor (32:4). And there are countless other verses with similar meanings to these.

No entity other than God possesses the necessary qualities to demand our unqualified submission. Therefore, it is not appropriate to submit to anyone or anything other than Him, unless that submission is ultimately directed towards God. Any respect, reverence, or allegiance directed to anyone else must ultimately be oriented towards Him. As God states in the Qurʾan, those who follow the M essenger, the uninstructed prophet … those who believe in him, honor him, and help him and follow the light that has been sent down with him, they are the felicitous (7:157). He also says, Your guardian is only Allah, His Messenger, and the faithful who maintain the prayer and give the zakat while bowing down (5:55). Elsewhere, it is written, But the faithful, men and women, are comrades of one another: they bid

what is right and forbid what is wrong … (9:71), and And whoever venerates the sacraments of Allah—indeed that arises from the Godwariness of hearts

(22:32). Hence, in Islam, there is no submission to anyone other than God unless this submission ultimately returns to Him and is intended for Him. How did idolatry originate, and how did it begin?

As we established in the previous section, human beings have an innate desire to make abstract concepts substantial and shape intangible ideas into tangible forms through representation and imagery. At the same time, humans are instinctively drawn to submit to any superior, dominating force and to be obedient to its commands.

This is why we see that the spirit of polytheism and idolatry has historically prevailed in human societies. It is a phenomenon that seems almost

impossible to prevent or avoid, even in modern, advanced societies, and even in those societies explicitly founded on the rejection of religion altogether. In these societies, we can see the erection of statues and images of

people, the reverence and respect shown towards them, and the degree of submission to them calls to mind the idolatrous practices of the very earliest times and earliest humans. Nevertheless, today there are hundreds of

millions of idolaters—in one form or another—on the face of the Earth, residing in its east and west.

With this in mind, we might hypothesise that idolatry among humans began with them making of statues of great men and raising up their likenesses, especially after their death, to serve as a memorial to them. Narrations from the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household support this idea. For example, in Tafsīr al-Qummī and ʿIlal al-sharāʾiʿ, it is narrated from Imām al-Ṣādiq, commenting on the verse of the Qurʾan: They said, ‘Do not abandon your gods…’ (71:23), that he stated: ‘They used to worship God, but when they died, their people were grieved. Then Satan—may he be cursed by God!—came to them and suggested, ‘Why not make statues in their image? Then you can look at them, find comfort in them, and worship God.’ He then made idols resembling them, and the people continued

to worship God, but also looked to these idols. When the winter and rains came, they took the idols into their houses.

They continued to worship God until that generation passed away.

W hen their children grew up, they said, “Our forefathers used to worship these idols.” Thus they started worshipping the idols instead of God. This is what God Almighty meant when He said, They said ‘… Do not abandon Wadd, nor Suwa’ (71:23).

History records that, in ancient Rome and Greece, the master of a house would be worshipped in his own home and, when he died, an idol was made in his honor for his household to worship. Many kings and great men were also deified by their people. For example, the Qurʾan mentions Nimrod, the king who lived at the time of Abraham and debated with him about his Lord, and Pharaoh, who was the enemy of Moses. This is evident in today’s places of idol worship, as well as in the ancient artefacts preserved from various religions which practice idolatry; there idols of many great religious figures, like the statues of Buddha and many Brahmin figures and others.

Their making of idols for the deceased and worshipping them, at the very least, show that these peoples did not believe that life ended with death but that people’s spirits endured and they could continue to influence events and care for their families as they did during their lives. In fact,

in some cases they might be thought to have become more powerful and infiuential because they were freed from the confines of material existence and limited from corporeal limitations. Consider the case of Pharaoh: He worshipped idols while he himself was considered a god and worshipped by his own people. As God said: “The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said: The elite of Pharaoh’s people said, ‘W ill you leave M oses and his people to cause corruption in the land, and to abandon you and your gods?’ (7:127). Taking up idols as deities:

Creating statues for human beings seems to have stimulated the idea of creating an idol for God, even though people had not habitually created a physical representation of God thus far, as He is beyond definition or imagination. This fact seems to have deterred people from creating an idol for Him. Instead, they took divergent approaches, with each person focusing on what mattered to them most in the visible cosmic order, seeking to

worship God through the mediation of the entity they believed God had delegated for managing that specific aspect of their existence.

For instance, peoples who lived along the coastlines worshipped the god of the sea, hoping to benefit from its bounty and to be spared from floods and tumultuous waves. People who inhabited valleys worshipped the god of the valley, while warriors worshipped the god of war, and so forth. In this way, it was not long before each individual fashioned a deity according to their own preferences, imagining for it a specific form and shape, and crafting it from metal, wood, stone, or some other material. It is reported that the Banū Ḥanīfa tribe from Yamāma made an idol out of date cakes, which they ended up eating during a period of drought and hunger.

Equally, when a person came across a beautiful tree or stone, they might be inclined to worship it. They often sacrificed sheep or camels, smearing the blood on their chosen idol. If their livestock fell ill, they would bring it to the idol and rub it against it. M any trees were treated as deities and seen as sources of blessing, thus people were careful not to harm these trees by cutting or breaking them. Instead, they would seek to propitiate them with offerings, vows, and gifts.

This explosion of polytheism led people to diverge widely in their practices relating to idols, to the extent that these could hardly be captured systematically or fully accounted for. However, a common belief among idol worshippers was that they treated these idols as intercessors who would plead with God on their behalf to bring them good fortune and ward of evil. Some people may have even viewed the idol as a deity in its own right, independent of God and not just an intercessor with Him. Others may have viewed it as an intercessor but placed it before or above God Himself. For example, the Qurʾan recounts in the verse: But what is for their partners does not reach Allah, and what is for Allah reaches their partners (6:136). Some idolaters worshipped angels, others worshipped jinn, some worshipped fixed stars like Sirius, and a group considered the planets (which

they believed were ‘wandering stars’) as gods. All of these practices have been touched upon in the Qurʾan, and they did all of this either out of desire to obtain benefit from these false deities or in order to ward of  their perceived harm.

It was rare for people to worship a deity other than the One God without creating an idol to which they directed their worship. W henever they

chose something as an intercessory being, they created an idol for it from wood, stone, or metal. They fashioned it into a representation of what they imagined it to embody in terms of life, creating it in the form of a human or an animal, even if the entity the idol represented didn’t necessarily align with this form, such as the fixed stars, planets, or gods of knowledge, love, provision, war, and so on.

The rationale behind adopting idols as partners to God lies in peoples belief that, because God is transcendent and beyond sensory perception, like the deities representing various species and all other non-material deities, or because His appearance isn’t fixed, like a star that transitions from rising to setting, making it difficult to focus on it whenever one wishes, it is necessary to create an idol to represent His attributes and qualities and to which worship can be directed. Hence, they would turn to the

idol as a means of reaching the deity whenever they desired.

Sabaeanism:

Even though all idolatry—roughly speaking—originates from the same source of seeking intercessors with God and worshipping their idols and images, and despite its dominance over the earth and the human world, as the Qurʾan relates about the nations of Noah, Abraham, and Moses, the differences between the various groups of idolaters because of their divergent whims and superstitions are so great that making an exhaustive list of all the various idol worshipping faiths and their unique practices is almost impossible. This is doubly so because most of these faiths do not rely on established principles or consistent, harmonious rules.

However, the Sabaeans, Brahmans, and Buddhists could all be counted as relatively organized, stable, and established sects of idol worship. As for the Sabaean religion, it is built on linking the phenomena and events of the terrestrial world to celestial bodies like the Sun, Moon, M ercury, Venus, M ars, Jupiter, and Saturn. They believe that these celestial bodies, with their associated spirits, govern the observable world, each

managing the events related to it as determined by the science of astrology. The cycle of worldly events is believed to repeat with the recurrence of the orbits of these celestial bodies indefinitely and without end.

The Sabaeans believe these celestial bodies serve as intermediaries between God and the observable world and that worshipping them brings humans closer to Him. Consequently, it is necessary to create idols and images for these entities, and then worship these idols and images to draw closer to them, in order to draw closer to the supreme Godhead.

Historical chronicles report that the person who established and refined the religious doctrines of the Sabaeans was Yudhāsaf, an astrologer who appeared in India during the reign of Tahmuras, the Shah of Iran.

He propagated his teachings and amassed a large number of followers during his lifetime. His teachings even spread to regions like Rome, Greece,

Babylon, and elsewhere. Temples and shrines were built, housing idols representing the various celestial bodies, each with their own set of rules, customs, sacrifices, and offerings that were managed by a dedicated priesthood. They have occasionally been accused of human sacrifice.

Sabaeans assert the oneness of God in His divinity, not in His worship. They believe He is transcendent above any deficiencies or imperfections, and believe that He must be described through negations rather than affirmations, such as saying He is not impotent, ignorant, mortal, unjust, or oppressive. They refer to these attributes the M ost Beautiful Names, but they do not claim that these names represent any absolute reality. We have discussed some of the Sabaean’s history in our commentary on the verse, Indeed the faithful, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabaeans (2:62) in the first volume of this work.

Brahmanism:

Bahmanism (or Hinduism), as we have already mentioned, is one of the most well-established idolatrous religions. It is perhaps the oldest human religion, as Indian civilization is one of the earliest human civilizations, which appears to have begun in pre-history. It is not clear when Indian peoples began to worship idols, but the classical historian al-M asʿūdī1 has said that Brahman was the name of the first king of India, who founded the country, established the foundations of civilization therein, and dispensed justice amongst its people.

If this is true, it is likely that Brahmanism originated sometime after him and was named in his honor. Many past nations have worshipped their kings and nobility, believing that they possessed supernatural authority and that divinity was manifested in them in some way. This is somewhat corroborated by the content of the Vedas, a body of scripture, which was

Buddhism1 can be seen as an effort to reform the teachings of Brahmanism. It was founded by Buddha Sakyamuni, who, according to the Chronicle of Ceylon, died in 543 B.C.E. Other sources disagree with this date, however, some by as much as two thousand years. This led some historians to suspect that the Buddha might be a mythical figure with no basis in historical fact. However, recent archaeological excavations appear to confirm his existence, and other newly found artefacts have revealed further information about his life and the teachings he gave to his disciples and followers.

Before founding the movement that is named after him, the Buddha belonged to a royal family as the son of King Suddhodana. However, he rejected worldly enjoyments and retreated from society in his youth. He spent many years of his life in solitude in the wilderness, dedicated to asceticism and spiritual discipline, until he achieved enlightenment. Emerging

from his solitude at the age of thirty-six, as reported, he called upon people to liberate themselves from misery and suffering and to attain supreme tranquillity and everlasting celestial life. He urged them to adhere to his teachings, cultivate noble ethics, renounce desires, and avoid vice. Reportedly, Buddha stated about himself with the utmost humility: ‘I

According to Buddhists, the Buddha’s teachings emphasized that nature is fundamentally empty and illusory, that non-existence pervades every place and every time, and that it is filled with deceit. However, they also believe that this very concept of non-existence removes all barriers between different human castes, peoples, and worldly nations, and makes the even the lowliest of worms brethren to the Buddhists.

Buddhists believe that the last words uttered by Sakyamuni were: ‘All component things in the world are impermanent.’ Their ultimate goal is the salvation of the soul from all pain and vanity. They believe that the endless cycle of reincarnation ends or ceases by preventing the soul from being born again, which is achieved by purifying it from all desire— even the desire to exist.

These fundamental principles of Buddhism are explicitly present in its earliest teachings recorded in the Arya Saccani or Four Noble Truths) They are ascribed to the Buddha and were reportedly mentioned in his first sermon, which he delivered in a deer park near Benares.

The Four Noble Truths concern the nature of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation. The first truth is that suffering is birth, ageing, illness, death, encountering what is unpleasant, separation from what is loved, and not getting what one desires. The second truth is that suffering is caused by carnal desires and emotional cravings. The third truth is the path to the cessation of all such desires and wants. The path to cessation consists of eight divisions (the Noble Eightfold Path): right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This forms the core of the Buddhist faith, which can be found inscribed on many structures and recorded in several books.

The essence of Buddhist morality is to avoid all base things, do all things that are good, and cultivate the mind.

This is what has been handed down from Buddha’s teachings. Aside from this, the rituals, sacrifices, priesthood, philosophies, and other mysteries were added over time and throughout the ages. These additions

include remarkable sayings and opinions on the creation of the world, its organization, and other matters.

It is said that Buddha never spoke of God, not out of disregard for the fact of His existence or a denial of it, but because he devoted all his efforts to preparing people to renounce the allure of worldly life and to develop an aversion for this fieeting abode.

Pre-Islamic Arab idolatry

The pagan Arabs were the first idol worshippers to be challenged by Islam, which called for monotheism against their widespread polytheism. During the pre-Islamic period, most Arabs lived in nomadic tribes. The more cultured among them, like the Yemenis, were essentially nomadic in nature, governed by a mix of diverse customs and traditions, which were borrowed from their powerful neighbors such as the Persians, Romans, Egyptians, Abyssinians, and Indians. These customs included their religious practices.

The ancient ancestors of these Arabs—the “original” Arabs, you might say—such as the ʿĀd, Iram, and Thamūd, were pagans, as God Almighty narrates in His Book about the people of Hūd and Ṣāliḥ, and about the dwellers of Madyan and the people of Sheba in the story of Solomon and the Hoopoe. That was the case until the arrival of Abraham with his wife Hagar and their son Ishmael in the land of Mecca, which was a barren valley inhabited by the tribe of Jurhum. They settled there, and Ishmael grew

up, the city of Mecca was built, and Abraham built the Kaaba, the Sacred House. He called people to his upright religion, which was Islam, and his call was answered in the Hijaz and surrounding regions. He instituted the ritual of the Ḥajj pilgrimage for them, as illustrated by what God Almighty told him in the Qurʾan: And proclaim the Ḥajj to people: they shall come to you on foot and on lean camels coming from distant places (22:27). Later, some of the Arab nomads converted to Judaism through their interactions with the Jewish tribes who had settled in the Hejaz, while Christianity infiltrated some regions of the Peninsula, and Zoroastrianism in others.

Subsequently, conflicts arose between the descendants of Ishmael and the tribe of Jurhum in Mecca, eventually resulting in the dominance of the Ishmaelites and the expulsion of Jurhum from the area. Subsequently, ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy took control of Mecca and its surrounding territories. ʿAmr fell gravely ill, and some suggested to him that the hot springs in the Balqa region of Sham (Greater Syria) might offer a cure. Upon visiting these springs and regaining his health, he observed people worshipping idols there. He inquired about this practice, and was told that

they worshipped these idols, shaped after heavenly bodies and human figures, to grant them victory over their enemies and to bring them rain for their crops. Intrigued, he requested one of their idols, and was given Hubal. Upon returning to Mecca, he placed it in the Kaʿba. Along with him were also Isāfiand Nāʾila, two idols depicted as a couple— or as two youths, according to other sources. He called on people to worship these idols, and this practice took hold among his tribe, and they resumed idol worship after their period of monotheistic faith. They had previously been known as ḥanifs, followers of the Abrahamic faith, but while they retained the name, they abandoned the meaning, and the term came to refer to the pagans among them as well.

One factor that facilitated their shift toward polytheism was the reverence that all religions— including Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism,

and paganism combined—held for the holy Kaʿba. No one would leave Mecca without carrying a stone from the holy sanctuary to take with them its blessings and sanctity. W herever they settled, they would place the stone on the ground and circumambulate it in imitation of and out of love for the Kaʿba and the sanctuary that surrounded it.

This is how polytheism spread among the Arab Bedouins and those who had adopted the Arab lifestyle. Monotheists among them were rare and are scarcely mentioned in historical sources. The well-known idols they worshipped include Hubal, Isāf, and Nāʾila, introduced by ʿAmr b. Luḥayy who invited people to worship them, as well as al-Lāt, al-ʿUzza, M anāt, Wadd, Suwāʾ, Yāghūth, Yaʿūq, and Nasr. These eight idols are mentioned in the Qur’an, and the last five are said to have belonged to the people of Noah in particular.

In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī narrates via a chain of transmission going back to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ashall, a vendor of carpets, who narrated from Imām al-Ṣādiq: ‘Yāghūth was placed facing the entrance of the Kaʿba, with Yaʿūq on its right and Nasr on its left.’

The narration also mentions: ‘Hubal was on the roof of the Kaaba, and Isāfiand Nāʾila were stationed on Ṣafā and M arwa.’ In Tafsīr al-Qummī, we read: ‘Wadd was an idol of the tribe of Kalb, Suwāʿ was for that of Hudhayl, Yāghūth for the tribe of Murād, Yaʿūq for the tribe of Hamdān, and Nasr for the tribe of Huṣayn.’

The religion practiced by the pre-Islamic Arabs contained traces of Sabaean teachings, such as bathing to purify oneself following sexual intercourse and other such practices.

It also contained elements of Brahmanism, such as belief in world eras and the in time as the ultimate reality. They say, ‘There is nothing but the life of this world: we live and we die, and nothing but time destroys us’

(45:24). Some mention that this is the belief of the materialists who deny the existence of a creator altogether.

There were traces of the original religion of Abraham, such as circumcision and the Ḥajj pilgrimage. However, these had been mixed with pagan

practices such as touching the idols around the Kaʿba, circumambulating the Kaʿba naked, and the polytheistic invocations they would recite, such as: ‘I come to you, O Allah, I come to you. You have no partner, except your partner. He is yours and all that is his is yours.’

They also innovated other practices, such as belief in the baḥīra, the sāʾiba, the waṣīla, and the ḥām, belief in the sadā, the ḥām, al-anṣāb (sacrificial alters), and al-azlām (diving arrows), among other practices mentioned in historical records. We have explained the meanings of the baḥīra, the sāʾiba, the waṣīla, and the ḥām in our commentary on verse 5:103, and of the anṣāb and azlām in our commentary on verses 3 and 90. Islam’s defence of monotheism and its confrontation with polytheism

Throughout the ages, the divine message has continuously confronted idolatry, stood up against it, and called people to follow the path of monotheism. This is what we find God has recounted in the Qurʾan in the stories

of prophets and messengers such as Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Abraham, Jethro, and M oses; this is also referenced in the stories of Jesus, Lot, and Jonah. The most comprehensive statement in this regard is the verse: W e did not send any messenger before you but We revealed to him that ‘There is no god except M e; so worship M e’ (21:25).

The Prophet Muḥammad began his public mission by calling the idol worshippers of his people to monotheism using wisdom, preaching, and arguing in the best of ways. However, his appeals were met with mockery, persecution, and severe torment for those who followed him. This state of affairs compelled a group of the early Muslims to abandon their homes in Mecca and seek refuge in Abyssinia. The idol worshippers of Mecca then conspired to assassinate the Prophet, which led him to emigrate to M edina, followed by many of the believers.

However, even though he had left behind his home, his enemies would not relent. They waged war on the Muslims, fighting them at the Battles of Badr, Uḥud, the Trench, and in numerous other armed confrontations until God granted His Prophet a decisive victory over them with

the conquest of Mecca. The Prophet then purged the Sacred House and the Sacred Precinct of their idols, breaking the graven images erected in and around the Kaʿba. It is said that Hubal, the largest of their idols, was placed atop the Kaaba, and ʿAlī was ordered to climb up and cast it to the ground. This idol, as they claim, was subsequently buried at the threshold of the mosque’s entrance.

Islam has been particularly diligent in abolishing idolatry, purging people’s hearts of any thoughts leading to it, guiding minds away from even contemplating it. This is evident in the fundamental teachings, noble morals, and legal precepts that Islam promotes. It establishes a fundamental belief in monotheism, that there is no god but God, with His most beautiful names, who is the Lord of everything. He alone possesses the primordial

existence that is independent of anything else, and He is Self-Sufficient, in no need of the worlds or their denizens. Everything other than Him begins with and returns to Him and is dependent on Him for its existence and survival. Thus, anyone who attributes any form of independence to anything besides Him, whether in its essence, its attributes, or its actions, is considered a polytheist according to this criterion.

Islam calls on people to rely on God and place their trust in God, to accept God’s sovereignty, love for the sake of God, hate for the sake of God, and to dedicate all of their deeds to God. It prohibits them from relying on anything other than God, placing their trust in others, feeling secure with the outward causes of this world, or having hope in anyone other than Him, or from behaving arrogantly or vainly. All these things involve attributing independence to entities other than God, which leads to polytheism and idol worship.

Equally, Islam prohibits people from prostrating themselves to anything other than God, creating statues that cast shadows, or drawing living

beings. It forbids obedience to anyone other than God or heeding them in their commands and prohibitions unless such obedience is ultimately directed to obeying God, as is the case with obeying the Prophets and religious leaders. It also prohibits contriving new things in matters of religion

and following in the footsteps of Satan.

The traditions that have come down to us from the Prophet and the Imāms of his Household consistently state that polytheism (shirk) has both blatant (jalī) and hidden (khafī) forms, that it also has many levels and only the truly dedicated can avoid entirely. The most hidden form of polytheism is said to be harder to perceive than the sound of an ant’s footfall on smooth stone in the darkest night. It is reported in al-Kāfī, from Imām al-Ṣādiq, concerning the verse of the Qur’an: … the day when neither wealth nor children will avail, except him who comes to Allah with a sound heart,’ (26:88–89): ‘The sound heart is one which meets God without anyone besides Him in it. Every heart that contains polytheism or doubt is fallen. Their asceticism in this worldly life is only intended to allow their hearts to focus on the afterlife.’

Also, it has been reported that worshipping God out of a desire for paradise is the worship of hirelings, and worshipping Him out of fear of hellfire is the worship of slaves, while the true essence of worship is to worship Him out of love for Him, and that this is the worship of the noble (kirām). This is a hidden spiritual station that only the purified can attain. Several of these traditions have been presented in previous sections of this book.

The entirety of the Prophet’s method was founded upon the principle of monotheism and the denial of partners to God. Moreover, God

Almighty has commanded that the Prophet’s methods, which He has ordered him to adopt and follow in human society, be based on the following verse: Say, ‘O People of the Book! Come to a word common between us

and you: that we will worship no one but Allah, and that we will not ascribe any partner to Him, and that we will not take each other as lords besides Allah.’ But if they turn away, say, ‘Be witnesses that we are muslims’(3:64). God has also criticized the People of the Book for allowing pagan beliefs and practices to infiltrate their religion: Say, ‘O People of the Book! Do not unduly exceed the bounds in your religion and do not follow the fancies of a people who went astray in the past, and led many astray, and (themselves) strayed from the right path’(5:77).

Moreover, God rebukes them in the following terms: They have taken their scribes and their monks as lords besides Allah, and also Christ, M ary’s son; though they were commanded to worship only the One God, there is no god except Him; He is far too immaculate to have any partners that they ascribe! (9:31).

The Prophet treated all people equally when applying the divine laws and enforcing God’s bounds. He bridged the gaps between different social classes such as the ruler and the ruled, the leader and the led, the servant and the served, the rich and the poor, men and women, the noble and the humble. And he established the principle that there is no honor, pride, or rule for any person over another except by virtue of their piety, and judgement belongs to God alone.

The Prophet distributed wealth equitably and forbade the powerful from displaying their strength in a way that would harm or dispirit the weak and abased, such as the rich fiaunting their wealth before the poor and needy, and rulers and leaders exercising their power over their subjects arbitrarily.

The Prophet lived as one of the people, distinguishing himself from them neither in food, drink, clothing, seating, walking, nor anything else. A summary of his life can be found in the final part of the sixth section of this book.

In this context, we will weigh the teachings of the Qurʾan by comparing them to the doctrines of Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, and Christianity, in a broad and comprehensive manner across various topics, in a scholarly and analytical fashion.

The concept of Reincarnation among the Pagans:

One of the primary beliefs that informs the foundations of Hinduism, as well as Buddhism and Sabaeanism, is that of reincarnation. This doctrine holds that the cosmos is continually subjected to cycles of creation and destruction. The observable world which we inhabit, as well as its various parts, is believed to have been formed from a previous world, and this cycle repeats indefinitely. This world will decay as its parts continue to do so, and a new world will be formed from it, and so on ad infinitum. The human being lives in each of these worlds based on whatever they have acquired in a preceding world. Those who do good deeds and cultivate noble virtues will, after death, attach their souls to a blissful body and live in happiness as a reward in their next cycle. Conversely, those who are overly attached to the material world and follow their desires instead of cultivating virtue will inhabit a wretched body after death, suffering various kinds of torment. The only exception to this cycle of death and rebirth are those who

recognise Brahman and unite with him. Such individuals escape from the cycle of death and rebirth and return instead as eternal, timeless entities that embody splendor, joy, life, power, and knowledge, and who are immune to annihilation and destruction.

Based on this, it is a religious duty for humans to believe in Brahman (who is the source of everything, analogous to God) and draw closer to him through sacrifices and acts of worship. They should adorn themselves with noble virtues and perform righteous deeds. If one’s worldly desires subside and they cultivate noble qualities, engage in good acts, and recognise

Brahman through self-awareness, they become a Brahmin and unite with Brahman, achieving a state of oneness. This is the greatest form of happiness and purest form of life. If one fails to attain this level in their current

life, they should still believe in him and do good deeds to find happiness in their subsequent life, which is their next life.

However, since Brahman is an absolute entity, encompassing everything and not encompassed by anything else, he is too high and exalted

for human beings to comprehend, except through negating all imperfections from him, or to approach directly through worship and sacrifice.

Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to draw closer to him through worshipping his deputies and the most potent of his creations so that they

may intercede with him for us. These are the deities who Hindus worship besides God through their idols. Within their multitude are beings

we would recognise as angels, jinn, or the spirits of holy men. The jinn are worshipped out of fear of the harm they can cause, while others are worshipped in hope of their mercy and fear of their wrath. Among their number are beings who are recognized as the consorts, sons, and daughters of God Almighty.

This is a summary of the doctrines of Brahmanism as taught by the Brahman scholars themselves.

However, the contents of the Upanishads1, which constitute the fourth section of the sacred Vedas, does not entirely agree with the general outline of their faith given above, even if the Brahman sect scholars teach it.

A critical investigator finds that the message of the Upanishads, which convey divine teachings (even if they do describe the divine world and matters related to it, such as the divine names, attributes, and actions— including creation, sustenance, life-giving, death, and the like— in ways akin to

the descriptions of physical materialistic matters like division, dispersal, stillness, movement, transition, settlement, unification, greatness, and smallness, among other physical-material states) explicitly state in certain parts that Brahman is an absolute, transcendental entity, beyond the reach of even the most beautiful names and supreme attributes of life, knowledge, and power, and utterly devoid of attributes of deficiency and the

physical-material characteristics, and there is nothing like unto it. They clearly state that the transcendent One is a unique entity, not born of anything, and has not given birth to anything, and there is nothing comparable or equivalent to Him in any way.

They also assert that truthfully, that none other than He should be worshipped, and no one else should be approached through offerings and sacrifices. Rather, He alone, without any partner, is deserving of worship. M oreover, they frequently affirm the truth of resurrection and state that He is the ultimate end to which all creation will ultimately return. They describe the rewards and punishments of deeds after death in a manner that does not preclude the possibility of being understood as referring

to the intermediate state (Barzakh) rather than to reincarnation.

It is particularly telling that these philosophical texts do not make any mention of idols or deities besides Brahman, let alone advocate worshipping

What we have cited from the Upanishads—and there is much more we have omitted—are, without a doubt, sublime truths and veritable knowledge that are in harmony with our innate human nature. As you can see,
