In fact, careful consideration leads us to the conclusion that these texts were actually lofty truths revealed to select individuals who were close to God. These individuals then conveyed what they discovered to some of their disciples, although they often spoke symbolically and used parables to illustrate their teachings.

These teachings, only grasped by the few, became the foundation upon which the everyday life— which constitutes the religion embraced by the general public— was based. These are profound insights, comprehensible only to a few knowledgeable individuals due to their elevated nature that surpass the physical and imaginative levels of human understanding, which is how the majority perceive things. Their intricacy challenges untrained intellects that are not accustomed to divine knowledge.

This knowledge, exclusive to the minority, and denied to the majority, is essentially a humanistic religion. However, we must be careful in our conclusions, because our God-given human nature also fosters societal engagement. To disconnect one group of people from others based on religious beliefs contradicts this human instinct and the divinely instituted cosmic order. This, indeed, is to abandon the path of reason, which is one of the three ways of attaining true knowledge—namely, divine revelation, mystical insight, and rational thought. Among these, intellect is the

most commonly used and the most essential for human life in this world. Divine revelation is granted only to the infallible prophets, and spiritual insight is accessible only to the most devoted of individuals who possess firm conviction. Yet, everyone, including those who receive revelation and insight, must employ rational argument in all aspects of worldly life. To do otherwise means to impose blind conformity on all aspects of human society and human fiourishing— beliefs, morals, and actions— which leads to the downfall of humankind.

M oreover, to eschew the use of reason reinforces the tradition of subjugation within human societies, and this is evidenced by extensive historical

experiences of human civilizations that have lived under the yoke of idolatrous religions or have followed the tradition of subjugation by worshipping lords other than God.

The Universality of these Dangers Among All Religions Other mainstream religions, despite their claim to monotheistic beliefs, have not been immune to the pitfalls of idol worship, leading them to encounter the same problems that the religion of Brahmanism faced, especially the three major issues mentioned above.

For example, Buddhism and Sabaeanism clearly exhibit these problems, and history testifies to this fact. Some of their beliefs and practices have already been mentioned.

As for the Zoroastrians, they attribute divinity to Ahura Mazda, but they also revere Yazdan, Ahriman, the angels entrusted with divine affairs, the sun, fire, and other things. History tells us of the servitude and class differences that prevailed in their societies as well. Careful reflection leads us to conclude that these issues arose due to the distortion of their original faith. It has been reported that the Prophet said about them: ‘They had a prophet whom they killed, and a book which they burned.’

Regarding the Jews, the Qurʾan frequently condemns their actions, their distortion of God’s book, and their practice of taking their scholars as lords beside God, as well as the misfortunes God afflicted them with due to their straying from the natural order and immoral behaviors.

As for the Christians, we have extensively discussed their deviations in their beliefs and practices in the third part of this book. If you wish, review the prologue of the Gospel of John and Paul’s letters in relation to the rest of the Gospels, and complement it with a review of the history of the Church. A full treatment of this is beyond the scope of our present discussion.

Therefore, an in-depth investigation into these matters leads us to conclude that the general misfortunes faced by religious societies across the human world are the legacy of the original idolatry. This idolatry took divine knowledge and supreme truths, used them as the basis of religious norms, and imposed these without recourse to reason on the understanding of the common folk which is mainly inclined towards sensory and

perceptible things. This had the expected results.

How did Islam address these erroneous beliefs?

The approach Islam adopted in reforming these fiawed doctrines is by presenting the divine truths in a clear and straightforward language that was digestible and comprehensible to the minds of ordinary people. Therefore, the teachings of Islam were such that people could apprehend them as if through a veil or receive them in a suitable garb. This makes these teachings appropriate for the common folk, while those with special insight can still gain direct access to them in their unveiled and manifest splendor, without the need for such mediation. Such people are the convinced believers who constitute the ranks of those blessed by God: the prophets, the

truthful, martyrs, and the righteous— very fine company indeed. God says, By the Manifest Book: We have made it an Arabic Qurʾan so that you may apply reason, and indeed it is with Us in the Mother Book (and it is) surely sublime and wise (43:2–4). He also says, This is indeed a noble Qurʾan, in a guarded Book,—no one touches it except the pure ones—(56:79). Moreover, the Prophet himself has said, ‘We, the company of the prophets, were commanded to speak to people according to the capacity of their intellects.’

Islam guarded against the dangers of idolatry and polytheism at the level of monotheism by affirming that nothing was independent in its essence or attributes except God Almighty, who is the Sustainer of all things. It presented an understanding of divinity that avoided the extremes of both anthropomorphism and unknowability. God was described as living, but not with a life like ours; knowing, but not with a knowledge like

ours; powerful, but not with a power like ours; hearing, but not with a hearing like ours; and seeing, but not with a sight like ours. In sum, there is nothing like unto Him, and He is greater than can be described. Despite this, people were instructed not to assert anything about Him without knowledge and not to adhere to a belief unless it is based on a rational proof that made sense to their minds and intellects.

In doing so, Islam managed to present religion equally to both the masses and the spiritual elite. Secondly, it allowed the healthy intellect to operate without squandering this divine gift. Thirdly, it brought together different classes in human society to the greatest degree possible without favoring one over another or prioritizing one and neglecting another. God says, Indeed this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord. So worship Me (21:92). And He says, O mankind! Indeed We created you from a male and a female, and made you nations and tribes that you may identify yourselves with one another. Indeed the noblest of you in the sight of Allah is the most Godwary among you (49:13).

This is merely a summary; more detailed arguments can be found dispersed throughout this commentary.

Supplications, Intercession, and Visitation One might suspect that the contents of some of our supplications, seeking intercession through the Prophet and his Household, invoking God in their name, visiting their graves, kissing them, seeking the blessings of the soil around them, and venerating their relics, is a form of idolatry or polytheism and, therefore, prohibited. One might argue that this kind of devotional orientation bestows a divine hue to something other than God and that this is idolatry. The idolaters committed polytheism because they said about their idols: ‘These are our intercessors before God,’ and they said, ‘We only worship them to bring us closer to God.’ Therefore, so the argument goes, it does not matter what you venerate besides God, whether it is a prophet, a saint, a tyrannical king, or anyone else; all of this is idolatry.

However, what this person has overlooked, firstly, is that affirming the causal power of something other than God, whether material or otherwise, is self-evident and undeniable. God, in the Qurʾan, has ascribed all manner of causal powers to beings other than Himself. Moreover, denying the

causal efficacy of anything other than God completely undermines the universal law of cause and effect, which is the foundation of all the proofs for the existence and oneness of God—to deny the law of causality would, therefore, to be deny monotheism. Of course, one can deny that anything has causal power that is independent from God. However, to deny that anything other than God has any causal power whatsoever is to deny what is self-evidently real and known innately to all human beings.

On this basis, we can understand the meaning of God’s words when He discuses the intercession of others with Him in the verse: Those whom they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession, except those who are witness to the truth and who know (43:86) and His in the verse: He knows that which is before them and that which is behind them, and they do not intercede except for someone He approves of … (21:28).

And what about those who turn to God and invoke Him in the name of the Prophet and Imāms? God has said, Certainly Our decree has gone beforehand in favor of Our servants, the messengers, that they will indeed receive divine help, and indeed Our hosts will be the victors (37:171–173), and He has said, Indeed We shall help Our messengers and those who have faith … (40:51).

As for those who venerate them and show their devotion to them by visiting their graves, kissing them, and treating their soil as blessed, this is because they are signs of God and His symbols, holding to His saying: And whoever venerates the symbols of Allah—indeed that arises from the Godwariness of hearts (22:32). This is in addition to the verse of kinship and other statements from the Qurʾan and the Prophetic Sunna.

All of these are examples of seeking intercession with God through them. God has said,

In all of this, he seeks God’s intercession through them. As God has said, O you who have faith! Be wary of Allah, and seek the means of recourse to Him (5:35). By this, the act of seeking recourse to God (tawassul) is made legitimate, and the Prophet and Imāms, by virtue of their love, respect, and reverence, are made a legitimate means of recourse to Him. The essence of the matter lies not in the negation of loving something or revering it, nor in the denial of that love or reverence having a real effect. Therefore, there is no problem with seeking closeness to God by loving them and venerating them, and whatever effects this may have, as long this takes the form

of seeking intercession through them and not assigning them the power to act independently of God or to worship them outright.

Secondly, the one who makes the aforementioned argument fails to properly distinguish between worshipping someone other than God in the hopes that they will intercede on their behalf with God or bring them closer to Him, and worshipping God alone, while seeking intercession and nearness to Him through them. In the first case, they have assigned independent power to this other being and made it an object of worship aside

from God Almighty. This is a form of idolatry, as it involves associating a partner with God in worship. However, in the latter case, this being is not given any causal power independent of God and God alone is the object of their worship, without having any partner.

God has condemned the polytheists for their saying, ‘We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah’ (39:3) because they have

treated them as independent beings and made them objects of worship besides Him. If, on the other hand, they had said, ‘We worship God alone and hope that His angels, messengers, or saints will intercede for us by His permission, or that we seek closeness to God by respecting His symbols and loving His allies,’ they would not have been counted as disbelievers for doing so. This is because, had they said this, their partners would have served a similar function to the Kaʿba in Islam; it is a direction of worship rather than an object of worship. It is only God who is worshipped by turning to face it in prayer.

Moreover, I wonder what these people say about the Black Stone and what has been prescribed in Islam about touching and kissing it? And about the Kaʿba itself? Are all of these actions forms of idolatry that have been exempted from the prohibition? If so, the prohibition on idolatry is an undeniable rational judgement that does not accept special cases or admit exemptions, therefore any such exception would be invalid. On the other hand, if the devotion shown to the Black Stone is the purely monotheistic worship of God and the stone merely serves as a means and a direction, then what is the difference between this and other forms of seeking a means to God, if merely venerating it does not necessarily entail treating it as an entity that is independent of God and worthy of worship in its own right? In addition to this, in order to deny the validity of such acts of intercession, one would have to deny the validity of the verses about venerating

God’s symbols and loving the Prophet and his Household.
